title: Detection Strategy for Exfiltration Over Web Service
shortTitle: Detection Strategy for Exfiltration Over Web Service
summary: This detection strategy covers exfiltration of data through legitimate web services such as cloud storage, code repositories, paste sites and file transfer platforms, matching technique T1567. It matters because the destination is an approved service on a permitted port, so network blocking and domain reputation offer no protection, and because the volume and the actor are the only things that separate abuse from normal business use. The telemetry that makes it possible is web proxy and gateway logs with upload size and destination, cloud audit records for storage and sharing operations, endpoint file read activity for archives and sensitive documents, and data loss prevention alerts where they exist. It fails in practice because browser uploads and approved cloud sync clients produce identical records, so the detection depends on correlating a staged archive and a large outbound transfer with an account whose role does not justify it.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for large amounts of company data being sent to a public web service. Examples are cloud storage, file sharing sites or code hosting sites. The traffic uses normal web ports, so it does not stand out on the network.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers prefer to send data out through services you already allow. Blocking them would stop normal work, so you cannot simply close the door. This detection gives you a chance to notice the transfer while the account is still active. You can also learn which files left.
howItWorks: The web gateway records every upload with the destination service, the account and the number of bytes sent.
The endpoint records archive tools being run and the files they read from sensitive locations.
The cloud provider records storage upload and file sharing actions with the identity that performed them.
The platform joins the local archive activity and the outbound upload by host, account and time.
The rule compares the transfer size with the normal pattern for that user and that destination.
A large transfer by an unusual account raises an alert with the destination and the byte count.
beginner.example: Think of a factory gate pass. Lorries leave all day and that is normal. The guard only checks the paperwork against the load. A lorry with the heaviest load ever seen, driven by someone from the finance office, is the one worth stopping. A huge upload by an unusual user is that lorry.
takeaways: Allowed services cannot be blocked, so behaviour and volume are your control.
Correlate local archive creation with the outbound upload before you judge.
Know which accounts handle sensitive data so volume comparisons mean something.

objectives: Explain why exfiltration over legitimate web services is hard to block at the network layer
Identify the proxy, cloud audit, endpoint file access and data loss prevention telemetry needed
Describe how staging an archive locally and uploading it produces a recognisable sequence
Compare transfer volume against the normal pattern for a user, a destination and a role
Write a detection rule for web service exfiltration and tune it against backup and sync clients
dataSources: Secure web gateway and proxy logs recording upload method, destination host, user identity and bytes sent per request
Cloud audit records for storage object upload, file sharing link creation and repository push operations with the acting identity
Endpoint process and file access records for archive utilities and the sensitive directories they read
Data loss prevention or content inspection alerts recording sensitive data types leaving the environment
logic: The pattern is a local archive being created from a sensitive directory, followed within a short time by a large outbound upload from the same host or account to a public file sharing or storage service, often outside the user normal working hours. The fields that must be correlated are the user identity, the host, the archive creation event and its size, the destination domain or storage bucket, the bytes transferred, and the sensitivity of the source paths. The benign case is an approved backup, a support case bundle or a marketing team uploading campaign assets to a sanctioned repository; the malicious case shows an account with no business need, a destination never used by that group, and a transfer far above the ninety fifth percentile for that account.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Large upload to public file sharing service after local archive creation
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   service: proxy
# detection:
#   selection_upload:
#     destination_host|endswith: [file sharing domains, cloud storage domains]
#     bytes_out|gte: 52428800
#   selection_archive:
#     Image|endswith: [7z.exe, rar.exe, tar, zip]
#     TargetFilename|contains: [sensitive, finance, hr]
#   filter_approved_clients:
#     user_agent|contains: [approved-backup-agent]
#   condition: selection_upload and selection_archive and not filter_approved_clients
# level: high
falsePositives: Approved backup and disaster recovery agents that compress data and upload it to an offsite storage bucket on a schedule
Support engineers who collect diagnostic bundles into an archive and send them to a vendor file transfer portal
Marketing and media teams that upload large campaign assets to external sharing services as part of normal work
Developers who push a large repository or release artefact to a public code hosting service for a legitimate project
tuningNotes: Baseline outbound upload volume per user group and per destination for a month, then set the size threshold above the ninety fifth percentile for the groups you monitor rather than using one global value. Allow list the user agents and source hosts of approved backup and sync clients, and scope the rule to accounts with access to regulated data so that general staff activity does not fill the queue. Keep the archive creation correlation so that a large upload alone does not alert. Narrowing to sensitive data holders means a slow exfiltration by other accounts is invisible, so keep a separate weekly report of first time upload destinations per user for trend review.
